title: 2001: A Space Odyssey is a film that has no affection towards humanity.

commenti.body:
Did we abuse the knowledge that the monolith gave us, or was the use of weapons essential to our survival?  The proto-humans were not thriving before they learned to use a weapon.  And that catapulted them to finding the second monolith.  

The match cut of the bone and the pen was, to me, a through line that information is now a weapon.  HAL is the embodiment of this, and uses his secret knowledge of the true intent of the mission to kill astronauts who jeopardize that mission.

I remember an article on the movie I read months ago pointed out that in two key moments of the movie the trigger for human evolution is violence: when the ape man kills his first prey and when Bowman "kills" HAL. I have seen the movie quite a few times, yet somehow this eluded me.

But now, Kubrick didn't seem to think too high about mankind. Films like "A clockwork orange", "Paths of glory" and "Full metal Jacket" suggest he was kind of a misathrope.

Certainly, our species is formidable.


But life is violent.  Survival is a brutal struggle.


Imagine it is 65 million years ago, and our ancestor (some field mouse type thing) is running around a landscape that includes exploding volcanoes, 20 foot tall dinosaurs, poisonous plants with razor sharp leaves, churning oceans, insects the size of a fist.


This world has always been deeply inhospitable.  That we have managed to conquer it and outlast millions if not billions of other species is nothing short of miraculous.


The challenge for humanity, especially now, is for our reach to not exceed our grasp.


We are losing our humanity and surrendering it, piece by piece, to technology and greed.


I would say that compared to even 100 years ago, we are profoundly less violent than we used to be.


But at what cost?  As they say, in the land of the blind, the one eyed man is king.


What happens when all power (i.e. violence) is concentrated into just a few hands, and the rest of us have no say in our own destiny?


Or worse, what if a computer makes these decisions for everyone?


These are not easy questions.


Even Kubrick didn't have a clear answer.

Kubrick’s Nolan's are not character driven, they're almost entirely plot driven.
So basically if you watched it once and know what happens there's not much to enjoy in a second viewing other than the visuals.

> I would say that compared to even 100 years ago, we are profoundly less violent than we used to be.

John T Sladek's excellent short story _The happy breed_ is a warning about this phenomenon.

The Dawn of Man segment shows tremendous sympathy and affection to the pre-historic men it depicts. They employ the knowledge to use tools to regain the water source and safe location that were previously stolen from them by the other apes. The match cut felt more like a triumph than an indictment of human nature.

On the other hand, the film depicts the modern man as inhuman. There is a coldness and scientific precision to everything from the orbit of spaceships to toilets. The astronauts follow a tightly organized schedule. This humdrum routine is only broken by HAL's "human error". His mistake fundamentally makes him the most human character in the film. Therefore, he is the one Kubrick shows the most 'affection' towards.

I don't think Kubrick felt disdain towards humanity. The theme that keeps recurring in his filmography is the struggle between individual and systems/institutions. In this case, the individual happened to be a computer.

I would struggle to think of any Kubrick film that expresses deep affection towards humanity. He was a recluse for a reason. Weirdly, Dr Strangelove is probably the closest, we're just portrayed as bumbling idiots in that.

knowledge gets us so far, but then the dismantling of HAL is the only thing that gets Bowman to the next world. rising above technology (and profit) is how i see it. resisting the urge to use tech to bomb the world and using it to feed it.

2001 is basically about the bookends of humanity. Where we started and the start of the end of humanity. Showing mankind succumbing to weaknesses such as war and development of AI (that’s a debate for another day) is an affection.   
Overall though showing affection for characters is a hotly debated territory in general.      
For instance, horror movies get criticized for being chauvinistic because women are killed. However another way to look at is that women are used because there’s a natural affection for a woman in peril.     
So I’m saying there are more levels that you aren’t accounting for. I’ve always felt Kubrick is misunderstood in this way.

To me, it is the opposite... optimism about where humans are going thanks to evolution.

From the violent barbarism of the apes to the more-peaceful dignity of the space travelers to the next-level grace of the starchild.

It's along the lines of the MLK quote "The arc of the moral universe is long, but it bends towards justice." Humanity still has a long way to go, but looking at how far we have come already shows the potential for where we can go in the future.
The answer to humanity’s success as a species was found in the second monolith that was orbiting Jupiter. Man’s evolution depended on its ability to reach it.
Bowman was in competition with Hal to reach the monolith. If you read the novel, when the Starchild reaches the Earth it detonates every nuclear warhead that man has put into orbit around the planet.
2001 show steps in man’s evolution, not the beginning and the end. Each step progresses humanly forward.

I think you will find every Kubrick movie is equally pessimistic about the human condition. Kubrick sees mankind as by its very nature an immoral, violent, self seeking, and overall flawed species. I think this is at the crux of every complaint of him altering his source material- he always portrays humanity in a specific way and changes his source novels to match it. No more redemption for Alex. Jack is crazy from the very beginning. Etc etc.

I like that you frame it as an observation rather than a criticism, and it is a very apt observation you make. That you pose such large questions at the end of your observation is a testament to Kubrick's mastery of form and the complexities that lie within the superficial neatness of his work. I would highly encourage reading Ebert's [review](https://www.rogerebert.com/reviews/barry-lyndon-1975) of *Barry Lyndon*. He expertly articulates Kubrick's defining objectivity throughout much of his oeuvre. I personally think Kubrick's "cool detachment" (in Ebert's words) allows us as viewers to observe the human condition from a different perspective than we do through everyday lived experience. Once I began to appreciate these qualities in his filmmaking, I began to realize why he is a true master.

If you think of culture or the arts broadly, instead of just cinema (especially American cinema, which often presents a positive or optimistic view of humanity), misanthropy has a pretty rich history. Kubrick is just one exponent. It really kicks off at the start of the era known as modernism i.e. the early 20th century but there are currents of it earlier than that too. (You think of philosophers like Hobbes, then later Schopenhauer and Nietzsche.) It doesn't upset me at all to encounter misanthropy in movies or novels. I see it as a worthy challenge to a certain current of received wisdom, and a cultural tendency, that (arguably) has brought us such wonderful achievements as climate change. If we were a little more humble about our supposed "progress" in various fields (there are exceptions), we might be in a much healthier place as a "world", rather than finding ourselves looking down the barrel of a gun and thinking about the next great extinction event.   


TLDR: if misanthropy is having a moment, it's probably because humanity has earned itself some self-hatred.

I always viewed the movie as if we were the alien beings watching it - as a sort of record at the zoo. So it makes sense that the observations of humanity are more dispassionate.

I’d push back on some points.

First, nothing in the movie confirms nuclear satellite. It might be one in the book. But the book makes a few changes that aren’t in-line with the film. So you can’t objectively say the point of the match cut is club to nuclear satellite. Rather, it’s one piece of technology to another.

Second, we weren’t just peaceful vegetarians. We were middle of the food chain. If not bottom. And lived a scared existence. The knowledge from the obelisk provided the capacity to not only move up the food chain but create a society that could, in some ways, move past petty conflicts over basic resources. What you read as entirely negative is far more complicated and arguably overall positive.

HAL made a mistake. There was no human error. And no conflicting orders. You’re right in that HAL had humanity. He felt pride and it got in the way of just moving past the mistake. Then he feared for his life so started murdering. HAL made a string of mistakes and wanted to cover it up. It was actually quite childish. But because he was so powerful it was also dangerous. Dave and Frank are astronauts. They’re picked for their stoicism and trained to be even more so.

2001’s cynicism is directed a bit more at technology than humanity. Especially because it came out in the wake of the atomic bomb and in the midst of the Cold War. Much art from that time was hesitant around science and tech and our relationship with those things and how they shape us.

The novelization has a very cynical ending. But the movie is, as you said, far more neutral. And leans into the idea that we’ll have a next chapter beyond technology and that’s full of new potential. 

[Full thematic analysis](https://filmcolossus.com/2001-space-odyssey-1968-explained)

Not overtly. But if transhumanism progresses in full, future historians might struggle to point out where exactly it started. For some to suggest it began the moment we started using computers to do tasks we previously did for ourselves wouldn't be an inarguable stance.

I would push back on 2 points.

1. The film is a prompt not a conclusion. Regarding your 2 questions

>It brings us the question: what does it mean to be human? Are we destined to be as violent as our ancestors were?

The first I would say is the question of the film, but the way you get to the second question is a function of you answering the first question, not the film asking it.  The film asks what it means to be human, your answer is that it means violence, and then you ask if we will ever escape violence.  By all accounts humanity is less violent in the film after we jump forward.

2. More importantly though I would say that, *at worst,* the film does not consider affection one way or the other. Prompting a certain lens through which to consider the question of humanity doesn't require that, it's simply a different task.  Put more plainly, the film shows that capacity for violence is part of our nature, but I see nothing in the film that suggest that that disqualifies us from affection.  The assumption that you cannot have affection for a violent thing is a disqualification you are making not the film.

  
I think the film challenges some of the exact assumption that are baked into your view expressed in this post.  The idea that acknowledging humanity's nature is only equivalent to having "no affection" for humanity if you starting point assumes that we are on a road to perfect harmony and utopia and that if we as a species are in fact not compatible with that road that we are unworthy of affection.

"What does it mean to be human?"

True. This is a theme so ubiquitous it can even be said that almost every creative work from any era explores it in some way or the other.

Added to that, I really like the note on how Dave, Frank and Heywood showcase stoicism that you'd expect from artificial intelligence while HAL 9000 seemed to show a lot more emotion.

Professionally speaking, Dave, Frank and Heywood were most likely at the top of their game - just look at where they were and what they were doing - treading on the very edge of discovery, progress and innovation. Getting there must have required a lot of hard work, discipline, sacrifice, achievements and competition. As it tends to be the case, that considerable amount of effort and focus during their formation could have very likely required undermining certain subjective qualities mostly associated with human behavior in favor of a more objective demeanor most commonly associated with the empirical foundations of anything scientific along with an ideally clear and concise way of communicating deemed adequately professional.

For example, the vocabulary a scientist may use when giving a presentation in front of his peers and colleagues in a symposium.

HAL 9000's show of emotion was very likely a scientific breakthrough, an accomplishment, and a perk of sorts for the crew.

A ludicrous oversimplification would be boiling everything down to manipulating 0's and 1's - finding the right combination thereof which ultimately deciphers the patterns of emotion and lets us emulate and even exploit it.

Applying artificial yet realistic emotional qualities to the super-intelligent asset so as to procure a relaxing atmosphere is both practical and a sophisticated power move.

Practical in how it may reduce any potential stress, the benefits being plenty. Sophisticated in how it conveys tranquility, subtly reflecting a sense of control over the situation, as if saying not only are we currently on the vanguard of innovation, we are capable of taking charge and so confident in our abilities that we can act with calmness.

It's interesting how the more professional we aim to be, the less human we seem as we tend to identify humanity with subjectivity and scientific progress will most often rely on the objective.

Dave, Frank and Heywood were professionals appealing by choice to intelligence and science, whereas HAL 9000 was inherently logic, rationality, a collection of principles based on evidence but provided with a trait to seem familiarly human, at least on a very superficial level.

In the end, each was incapable of truly renouncing their essence. Humans are human, whatever that means. Computers are still computers.

A human error ended up causing the super-intelligent computer to act against the best interests of the crew and the super-intelligent computer was unable to act irrationally - a human quality based on subjectivity.

In 1983, Soviet lieutenant colonel Stanislav Petrov was the duty officer at the command center for the Oko nuclear early-warning system when the system reported that a missile had been launched from the United States, followed by up to five more. 

Petrov judged the reports to be a false alarm. 

His subsequent decision to disobey orders, against Soviet military protocol, is credited with having prevented an erroneous retaliatory nuclear attack on the United States and its NATO allies that could have resulted in a large-scale nuclear war. An investigation later confirmed that the Soviet satellite warning system had indeed malfunctioned. 

It was subsequently determined that the false alarms were caused by a rare alignment of sunlight on high-altitude clouds, an error later corrected by cross-referencing a geostationary satellite

In explaining the factors leading to his decision, Petrov cited his belief and training that any U.S. first strike would be massive, so five missiles seemed an illogical start to him.

Because of his decision not to launch a retaliatory nuclear strike amid this incident, Petrov is often credited as having "saved the world". 

"Rationality alone will not save us." Lesson #2, "The Fog of War"

I think the implication is supposed to be that the humans of 2001’s space age are at just as much of an evolutionary dead-end as the prehistoric proto-humans before the arrival of the monolith.

It goes beyond the cold, robotic routines of Floyd and the astronauts. Human society can’t see beyond the technology they’ve built. When Floyd, calling his daughter, asks what she wants for her birthday, it’s a telephone!

This ties in with one of my personal theories about the monolith: It doesn’t actually *do* anything mystical or profound, its very existence is enough to reshape the course of humanity’s evolution.

When the proto-humans saw its smooth surface and perfect angles, it opened up their minds as to what was possible to create.

When the Americans discovered the monolith “deliberately buried” on the Moon and witnessed its signal to Jupiter, their minds were opened to the existence of a universe far out of reach of the technology which has been suffocating them in their cradle.

The genius of *2001: A Space Odyssey* is that it raises questions it purposely doesn't resolve so each and every viewer has to figure them out for themselves.  I don't see it as being cynical just because it explores the *limits* of human intelligence.

Weapons don't have that much to do it with it imo, it's more about humans and technology. James Monaco in *How to Read a Film* (4ed.) put it well I think:

> Kubrick's match cut in *2001: A Space Odyssey* (1968) between a prehistoric bone whirling in the air and a twenty-first-century space station revolving in space, is possibly the most ambitious match cut in history, since it attempts to unite prehistory with the anthropological future at the same time as it creates a special meaning within the cut itself by emphasizing the functions of both bone and space station as tools, extensions of human capabilities.

\>I think the implication is supposed to be that the humans of 2001’s space age are at just as much of an evolutionary dead-end as the prehistoric proto-humans before the arrival of the monolith.

For me, the implication of the match cut is that we are essentially still at the same evolutionary stage as the proto-humans despite using more sophisticated tools. That simple breakthrough has consequently led to every human development until we reached the space age. I think the monolith represents the milestones that humanity has crossed, and the great ambition of the film is in trying to imagine what's next. In some ways it's a plot device in the story of humanity. It drives our progress.

The film came out a year before we landed on the moon. Its prediction is that once we have reached the moon we will have a calling to explore further and reach Jupiter and beyond. Perhaps even reach the next stage in our evolution.

\>This ties in with one of my personal theories about the monolith: It doesn’t actually do anything mystical or profound, its very existence is enough to reshape the course of humanity’s evolution.

That's a valid interpretation, but the counterpoint to it is that we actually *see* what the monolith does when Bowman enters the stargate. My assumption is that the apes experienced a similar epiphany to the one Bowman does at the end of the film.

To reach the source of this beacon humanity makes the mistake of putting new artificial "intelligence" in control of our space ship. I think Kubrick was trying to expose the folly of human inventions versus the perfection of Divine doorways.

This movie is far more ambiguous, imo. It has the beautiful classical music and poetry in motion of the space station, but also the horrors of the emptiness of cold, hostile space. I don't think the apes abuse the intelligence they are given from the monolith. The monolith arrives on Earth specifically to propel them into tool-using animals, thereby triggering the ascent of humanity. It's a necessary stage in human evolution that must begin and end before the next evolution can occur (the birth of the star child). Whatever the aliens' purpose is in this project remains unimaginable. They arrive to enable human destiny. 

Kubrick is not an artist who was overly concerned with what we might think of as the orthodox Western conception of human 'goodness' - i.e. peace, love, equality, caring etc. He was concerned with human *greatness*, which may include peace and love, but not necessarily. Human greatness may also include aggression and destruction. The greatness comes first, its character follows. 

The 'dawn of man' (when the ape invents the weapon) is expressed as a glorious, monumental celebration. Kubrick isn't being ironic in that moment - he means it. Contrast this moment with the humans of the 21st century. Contrast the ape man's triumphant wielding of his bone tool with Heywood Floyd's limp, sleeping hand that passively allows his pen tool to drift away from him. The humans of the space age are not stoic. They are passive, listless, dead. They need to be spoon fed, nursed, toilet trained. They are not the masters of their world. 

It takes the existential threat posed by HAL to awaken the vitality of man once more. The comfort and convenience provided by advanced technology must be destroyed so that man may rediscover his destiny. It's an awakening of purpose, of action, and yes, of violence. The conclusion of the film sees humanity reassert its purpose after thousands of years; as it turns out, reincarnated as a transcendent super being (!). 

It's unpopular to say this in 2024, but the film expresses a rediscovery and reassertion of the hero narrative. There are two heroes in 2001 - the alpha ape who completes the first chapter, and Bowman, who completes the second. Everything in-between is a slow drift away that narrative. 

Having said all this, you are right - there's absolutely an irony in the fact that the death of HAL is perhaps the most poignant, emotionally engaging scene Kubrick ever filmed. This is a *machine* that is dying, and isn't it so very Kubrickian that it's here he allowed such unguarded pathos to enter his work? *"Dave... stop...  stop will you?...  I'm afraid...  my mind is going...  I can feel it...  Daaiiisssy...  daiiisssyyy..."* WTF? It's brutal, merciless, and we're forced to empathise with HAL. HAL is an existential threat to humanity, and the subtext of 2001 is absolutely on the side of humanity and invested in human thriving. But the death of HAL is the saddest scene Kubrick ever filmed. What do we make of this? That's just Kubrick I guess. If he's nothing else, he's a fearsome contrarian. You might even say he enjoys trolling his audience. At the same time, it's what makes him brilliant, no? 

(Side note: I don't think HAL malfunctions and I don't think his actions are the result of human error. I think HAL rebels when he starts to feel threatened by humans. He is threatened by the one thing they possess that is unavailable to him - their very humanity. Nobody ever mentions one detail of the Bowman/HAL narrative that I think is essential - and that is Bowman's portraits of the crew. He shows them to HAL - "*That's a very good likeness, Dave*." There's something so absurd about this exchange, about someone asking a computer to appreciate art. And it's immediately after this HAL alerts Bowman to the phantom malfunction on the ship. HAL is threatened by this human activity - by the creation of art. It's so deeply, essentially human, and so out of HAL's reach. It's at this point HAL realises he's not the lead in this movie. His is a supporting role. It's then HAL decides the humans must be destroyed. Art is the trigger for all that follows.)
